title: React Native interview questions
tagline: Short answers to the questions that come up in almost every React Native interview.
intro: Each answer is the version you can say out loud in under a minute, with the one detail that shows you have actually used it.

sections.title: Architecture: the Bridge and the New Architecture
sections.summary: The question most likely to go deep.

blocks.caption: How JavaScript reaches the native side, before and after.

items.label: The Bridge
items.detail: Old: JS and native exchange JSON messages asynchronously over a queue
explain: The JavaScript thread runs app logic; the native thread draws UI. Every call between them is serialised to a JSON string and batched.
Example: a scroll event goes native → JSON → JS, and the resulting style update goes back the same way, a frame or more later.
That serialisation and the asynchronous hop are the bottleneck: heavy traffic means dropped frames.

items.label: JSI
items.detail: New: a C++ interface that lets JS hold native objects and call them directly
explain: JSI (JavaScript Interface) exposes C++ host objects to the JS engine. A call is a function call, with no JSON in between.
Calls can be synchronous when they need to be, such as reading a layout measurement during a gesture.

items.label: Fabric
items.detail: The new renderer, built on JSI, that can update layout synchronously
explain: Fabric keeps the UI tree in C++, shared by all platforms, and commits changes without waiting on the bridge's queue.
The payoff is responsiveness: fewer dropped frames and support for React's concurrent features.

items.label: TurboModules
items.detail: Native modules built on JSI and loaded lazily, on first use rather than at startup
explain: Under the bridge every native module was initialised at launch, used or not. TurboModules load the camera module only when the camera opens.
Faster startup is the headline benefit, and typed specs generated by Codegen catch mismatches at build time.

rows: Meta's open-source framework for iOS and Android apps in JavaScript and React. It renders real native views, not a web view, so code is shared and the UI still feels native.
ECMAScript 2015, the sixth edition of JavaScript: let and const, arrow functions, classes, promises and import/export modules.
JS is dynamically typed and checked at runtime. TS is a superset that adds static types checked at compile time, then compiles to JS; it catches type errors before they ship.
Both. ESLint enforces code-quality rules that prevent bugs, such as unused variables. Prettier only formats. ESLint says how to write it; Prettier says how it looks.
Functions that let function components use state and lifecycle, e.g. useState and useEffect. Call them at the top level only, from components or custom hooks.
A function whose name starts with use, e.g. useFetchData, that wraps built-in hooks so stateful logic is shared between components instead of copied.

sections.title: Redux, Context or Zustand
sections.summary: For global state, pick by size and update rate.

rows: Large apps that need predictable changes and time-travel debugging
Rarely changing values: theme, auth status

body: One line to end on: Context for simple, static state; Zustand for simple, changing state; Redux for large, regulated state.
